title: Practice Test 3
description: A full-length adaptive digital SAT practice test written by SAT Ustoz: 98 questions, two modules per section, with an explanation for every question.

questions.passage: The road to the village in the Nurata Mountains is so ______ that drivers must slow almost to walking speed at each of its many sharp bends.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: A road with many sharp bends twists back and forth, so it is **winding**. *Crowded* doesn't explain why drivers slow down at the bends.

questions.passage: Botanists were at first ______ about reports that the shrub could thrive in the salty soil around the old lakebed, since most plants in its family die when salt levels rise. Field surveys, however, confirmed that the shrub grows there in dense thickets.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: The botanists doubted the reports because related plants die in salty soil, and "however" shows the doubt was later proved wrong. Doubting a claim is what **skeptical** means.

questions.passage: Parrotfish scrape algae off coral with their beaklike teeth, grinding up bits of the coral itself in the process. The ground coral passes through the fish and comes out as fine white sand, so on some reefs parrotfish are a major ______ of new sand.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: The fish turn coral into sand, so they are where new sand comes from: a **source**. They consume coral, not sand, so *consumer* doesn't fit.

questions.passage: Jazz historian Odile Marchetti argues that the link between the two pianists' styles, often cited as proof that the younger player modeled his approach on the older one, is ______: the shared features she examines also appear in the work of dozens of other pianists of the period, so they could easily have developed independently.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Features shared by dozens of pianists are weak evidence of a direct link, so Marchetti finds the link **tenuous** (weak). *Conclusive* is the opposite, and *reciprocal* (mutual) misses her point, which is whether there was any influence at all.

questions.passage: Seagrass meadows cover only a tiny fraction of the seafloor, yet they hold a surprisingly large share of the carbon buried in ocean sediments. __The grasses' dense roots trap drifting particles and keep the seafloor from being stirred up, so plant material that settles in a meadow can stay buried for centuries.__ For this reason, some conservation groups argue that protecting seagrass is among the most effective ways to keep carbon out of the atmosphere.
questions.prompt: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It describes a threat that is causing seagrass meadows to shrink.
It presents evidence that challenges the claim made in the first sentence.
It compares seagrass meadows with other habitats that store carbon.
It explains how seagrass meadows are able to store the carbon mentioned in the previous sentence.
questions.explanation: The first sentence says the meadows hold a lot of carbon. The underlined sentence explains how: the roots trap material and keep it buried.

questions.passage: In many fast-growing cities, new apartment districts are built first and connected to public transit years later, by which time most residents have come to depend on cars. Urban planner Jasur Tillayev proposes reversing that order in the expanding cities of Central Asia: build the rail line first, then permit housing and shops within a ten-minute walk of each station. Residents who move into such districts, he argues, will build their travel habits around the train from the start instead of having to be persuaded to give up their cars later.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To argue that new apartment districts should not be built in fast-growing cities
To present a planner's proposal for the order in which new districts should be developed and the reasoning behind it
To describe the history of rail transit in the cities of Central Asia
To compare the cost of building rail lines with the cost of building roads
questions.explanation: The text describes the usual order of development, then Tillayev's proposal to reverse it and his reason: habits form around the train from the start.

questions.passage:
**Text 1**
Many popular histories of jazz describe improvisation as pure invention in the moment. On this view, a great soloist builds each solo from nothing while performing, and the solo's value lies chiefly in its originality.

**Text 2**
Musicologist Arlo Penhallow transcribed hundreds of recorded solos by three celebrated saxophonists and found that each player returned again and again to a personal stock of short phrases, which he recombined and varied from night to night. Penhallow argues that improvisation is better understood as the rapid, skillful rearrangement of practiced material, much as a fluent speaker forms new sentences from familiar words.
questions.prompt: Based on the texts, how would Penhallow (Text 2) most likely respond to the view of improvisation described in Text 1?
choices: By agreeing that a solo's value depends mainly on how original it is
By claiming that celebrated saxophonists rarely improvise during live performances
By arguing that it overstates how much of a solo is newly created during performance, since soloists draw heavily on phrases they have practiced
By suggesting that soloists who reuse phrases are less skilled than soloists who do not
questions.explanation: Penhallow found that solos are built from practiced phrases, which challenges the idea that a solo comes "from nothing." He still treats this as improvisation and calls it skillful, so the choices about rarely improvising or being less skilled misread Text 2.

questions.passage: When the town of Belgrav turned its central square from a parking lot into a pedestrian plaza, some shop owners worried that they would lose customers who arrived by car. A year later, a survey found that the number of people walking through the square had nearly doubled, and most shops reported higher sales than before. Many visitors said they now stayed longer because the square was quieter and had places to sit.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Most visitors to Belgrav's central square now arrive by car.
Shop owners in Belgrav have opposed every change to the town center.
Belgrav plans to turn its other parking lots into plazas.
Turning the square into a pedestrian plaza appears to have helped local shops, despite some owners' fears.
questions.explanation: The owners feared losing customers, but foot traffic and sales both rose, so the change helped the shops.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a short story. Kamola is helping her aunt repair fishing nets on the shore of a lake.

Kamola's fingers were clumsy at first, and the knots she tied slipped loose as soon as she pulled on them. Her aunt said nothing. She simply took the net back, retied each knot with three quick twists, and handed it over again. By late afternoon, Kamola noticed that her own hands had begun making the same three twists without being told, and that her aunt had stopped checking her work.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: By watching her aunt, Kamola gradually learns to tie the knots well enough that her aunt comes to trust her work.
Kamola's aunt grows frustrated with Kamola's clumsy knots and criticizes her repeatedly.
Kamola decides that repairing nets is too difficult and asks for a different task.
Kamola shows her aunt a faster way to tie the knots.
questions.explanation: The aunt teaches silently by example, Kamola's hands learn the three twists, and the aunt stops checking her work, which shows trust. The aunt "said nothing," so she does not criticize Kamola.

questions.passage: Agricultural researcher Sherzod Qodirov hypothesizes that rows of trees planted along the edges of wheat fields reduce water loss from the soil mainly by blocking dry winds rather than by shading the ground.
questions.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Qodirov's hypothesis?
choices: Fields bordered by trees produced more wheat than fields with no trees along their edges.
Soil moisture was nearly as high in fields bordered by low hedges, which block wind but cast almost no shade on the fields, as in fields bordered by tall trees.
Soil in shaded parts of the fields was cooler than soil in sunny parts.
Fields bordered by trees lost the most water during the hottest months of the year.
questions.explanation: Hedges block wind but give almost no shade. If they save nearly as much water as trees, blocking wind, not shade, must be doing most of the work.

questions.passage: Materials scientist Elif Durmaz and her colleagues mixed tiny polymer capsules filled with a liquid healing agent into concrete. When the concrete cracks, the capsules break open. Durmaz hypothesizes that the liquid released from the broken capsules, rather than the polymer used to make the capsule walls, is responsible for the concrete's improved ability to seal its own cracks.
questions.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Durmaz's hypothesis?
choices: Concrete containing filled capsules sealed its cracks faster in warm conditions than in cold conditions.
Concrete containing only the polymer used for the capsule walls sealed its cracks as well as concrete containing filled capsules.
Concrete containing filled capsules sealed its cracks, but otherwise identical concrete containing the same number of empty capsules did not.
Concrete containing filled capsules was slightly weaker under pressure than ordinary concrete.
questions.explanation: Empty capsules have the same polymer walls but no liquid. If only the filled capsules work, the liquid is responsible. The polymer-only result would point to the walls instead, which weakens the hypothesis.

questions.passage: Planners in the city of Dornholt recorded how many riders used each of four tram stops on an average weekday and how far, on average, those riders walked to reach the stop. The planners noted that the stop with the most riders was also the stop that riders reached with the shortest walk: ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: Station Square stop had 2,450 riders, who walked an average of 310 meters.
University stop had 3,020 riders, who walked an average of 260 meters.
Riverside stop's riders walked an average of 420 meters, farther than riders at any other stop.
Old Market stop had more riders than Riverside stop did.
questions.explanation: University has both the most riders (3,020) and the shortest average walk (260 meters), which is exactly the planners' point.

questions.passage: For centuries, many scholars accepted the idea that people see by sending rays out from their eyes toward objects. In the eleventh century, the scholar Ibn al-Haytham pointed out that looking at the Sun hurts the eyes and that a very bright light can leave an afterimage even after the eyes are closed. Since such effects are hard to explain if vision depends only on rays leaving the eye, Ibn al-Haytham concluded that ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: light must travel from objects into the eye.
the eye must send out stronger rays when it looks at bright objects.
the Sun must be much closer to Earth than scholars had believed.
afterimages must be caused by objects that are not actually present.
questions.explanation: Pain and afterimages show that something from outside acts on the eye, so light must enter the eye. Stronger outgoing rays would still not explain these effects.

questions.passage: In kelp forests along some coasts, sea urchins graze on kelp, and a species of sea star preys on the urchins. After a disease killed most of the sea stars in one region, urchin numbers rose sharply and large areas of kelp disappeared. In a nearby region, the same disease killed most of the sea stars, but the kelp forests remained largely intact. Divers there found that a large population of a predatory fish that also eats urchins had survived. These observations suggest that ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the predatory fish are more effective than the sea stars at finding and eating urchins.
the loss of one urchin predator may do less harm to kelp forests where other urchin predators remain abundant.
the disease that killed the sea stars did not reach the second region.
kelp forests recover quickly once urchin numbers begin to rise.
questions.explanation: The one difference between the regions is the surviving fish, which likely kept the urchins in check. The text never compares how well fish and sea stars hunt, and it says the disease did reach the second region.

questions.passage: The potters of the village dig their clay from a bank along the nearby ______ its fine, smooth texture lets them shape bowls with very thin walls.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: Both parts are complete sentences, so they need a semicolon. A comma alone creates a comma splice.

questions.passage: Al-Jazari's *Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices*, completed in ______ describes about fifty machines, including water clocks and pumps.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The phrase "completed in 1206" interrupts the sentence and opens with a comma, so it must close with a comma before the verb "describes."

questions.passage: Researchers studying a deep-sea glass sponge found that each of its needle-like spicules is built from dozens of thin layers of silica separated by a protein ______ an arrangement that allows the spicule to bend without snapping.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The words after the blank ("an arrangement that...") are not a complete sentence; they describe the layered structure, so a comma is needed. A semicolon must be followed by a complete sentence, and *glue, it is* creates a comma splice.

questions.passage: The images that the telescope's infrared camera captured during its first month of ______ revealed dust clouds that earlier instruments had been unable to detect.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: "The images...operation" is the subject and "revealed" is its verb. No punctuation should separate a subject from its verb.

questions.passage: Every morning, the stalls at Tashkent's Chorsu Bazaar ______ piled high with dried apricots, spices, and round loaves of bread.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The subject is the plural "stalls," so the verb is **are**.

questions.passage: In the mid-twentieth century, chemists at several laboratories worked to develop plastics that could withstand high temperatures. The ______ efforts produced materials now used in products ranging from cookware to spacecraft.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The efforts belong to several laboratories, so the plural possessive **laboratories'** is needed. *Laboratory's* refers to just one laboratory.

questions.passage: The trumpeter's recordings from the 1950s, along with a box of handwritten arrangements discovered in a Tashkent apartment last year, ______ given historians a fuller picture of the city's early jazz scene.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The subject is the plural "recordings." The phrase "along with a box..." does not change the number of the subject, so the verb is **have**. *Has* wrongly agrees with "box."

questions.passage: Mangrove roots form dense tangles that slow the movement of water along the shore. ______ mud and sand settle among the roots instead of being carried out to sea.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: Mud settling among the roots is a result of the roots slowing the water.

questions.passage: Many jazz pianists of the 1920s and 1930s played a steady "stride" pattern with the left hand, alternating low bass notes with chords. ______ bebop pianists of the 1940s largely abandoned this pattern, using the left hand only for occasional chords and leaving the bass line to the bassist.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: Bebop pianists did the opposite of the earlier pianists, so a contrast is needed.

questions.passage: The city's redesigned bus network cut average travel times by only a few minutes. ______ because the redesign also made buses arrive far more often, ridership rose by nearly a third within a year.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: The first sentence stresses a small benefit ("only a few minutes"), and the second describes a large gain in spite of it, so a concession like **Still** fits. *Thus* would wrongly present the rise in ridership as a result of the small time savings.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Al-Biruni was a scholar born in 973 in Khwarazm, a region in present-day Uzbekistan.
• He estimated the size of Earth by climbing a mountain and measuring the angle at which the horizon appeared to dip below a level line of sight.
• His result was remarkably close to modern measurements.
• He also wrote a detailed study of the sciences and customs of India.
questions.prompt: The student wants to explain how al-Biruni estimated the size of Earth. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Al-Biruni's estimate of the size of Earth was remarkably close to modern measurements.
Al-Biruni estimated the size of Earth by climbing a mountain and measuring the angle at which the horizon appeared to dip below a level line of sight.
Al-Biruni, a scholar from Khwarazm, was born in 973.
In addition to his work on Earth's size, al-Biruni wrote a detailed study of India.
questions.explanation: The goal is the method. Only this choice says what al-Biruni actually did; the choice about accuracy gives his result, not how he got it.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 2021, the cities of Vellmoor and Kestrey both made all bus rides free.
• In Vellmoor, bus ridership rose 25% in the first year.
• In Kestrey, bus ridership rose 9% in the first year.
• On Vellmoor's main routes, a bus arrived every 10 minutes.
• On Kestrey's main routes, a bus arrived every 30 minutes.
questions.prompt: The student wants to suggest a possible reason the two cities' results differed. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Although both cities made bus rides free in 2021, ridership rose far more in Vellmoor (25%) than in Kestrey (9%), possibly because Vellmoor's buses came three times as often.
In 2021, Vellmoor and Kestrey both made bus rides free, and ridership rose in both cities.
On Vellmoor's main routes a bus arrived every 10 minutes, while on Kestrey's a bus arrived every 30 minutes.
After Vellmoor made bus rides free in 2021, its ridership rose 25% in the first year.
questions.explanation: The goal needs both the different results and a possible cause. Only this choice links Vellmoor's larger rise to its more frequent buses. The choice about bus frequency gives a difference but never connects it to ridership.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Nitinol is an alloy of nickel and titanium developed in the early 1960s.
• It is a shape-memory alloy: after being bent out of shape, it returns to its original shape when warmed.
• Doctors use small tubes of metal mesh, called stents, to hold narrowed blood vessels open.
• A nitinol stent can be compressed to fit inside a thin tube for insertion and then expands to its original shape as it warms to body temperature.
questions.prompt: The student wants to explain how a property of nitinol makes it useful in medicine. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Nitinol, an alloy of nickel and titanium, was developed in the early 1960s.
Nitinol is a shape-memory alloy that returns to its original shape when warmed.
Because nitinol returns to its original shape when warmed, a stent made of it can be compressed for insertion and then expand inside a blood vessel as it reaches body temperature.
Doctors use small tubes of metal mesh, called stents, to hold narrowed blood vessels open.
questions.explanation: Only this choice connects the property (returning to shape when warmed) to the medical use (a stent that expands inside the body). The others give the property or the use, but not both.

questions.passage: The museum's oldest manuscript is so ______ that curators turn its pages only with a thin, soft spatula and never with their fingers.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Pages that must be handled so gently are easily damaged, or **fragile**.

questions.passage: Because the old bridge could no longer ______ the weight of heavy trucks, the city opened it only to cars, bicycles, and people on foot.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: The bridge was closed to trucks because it could no longer hold up their weight, so it could not **support** them.

questions.passage: Saxophonist Iris Kemal's recordings were largely ______ during her lifetime, selling only a few hundred copies, but jazz fans rediscovered them decades after her death and now consider them classics.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Selling only a few hundred copies and being "rediscovered" later means the recordings were ignored at first, or **overlooked**. *Celebrated* is the opposite.

questions.passage: Stainless steel resists rust because the chromium it contains reacts with oxygen in the air to form an extremely thin film, which ______ the metal underneath from further attack.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: The film is the reason the steel resists rust, so it protects, or **shields**, the metal underneath. *Exposes* is the opposite.

questions.passage: In 2011, high-speed trains called Afrosiyob began running between Tashkent and Samarkand, cutting the trip between the two cities to about two hours. Because a traveler can now leave Tashkent in the morning, spend the day in Samarkand, and be home the same evening, the trains have made day trips between the cities easy.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To compare the history of Tashkent with the history of Samarkand
To argue that more high-speed railways should be built in Uzbekistan
To explain how a new train service changed travel between two cities
To describe how the Afrosiyob trains were designed and built
questions.explanation: The text introduces the trains and then explains their effect: a shorter trip that makes day trips easy.

questions.passage: When a whale dies in the open ocean, its body usually sinks to the deep seafloor, where food is scarce. __There, a single carcass can feed a changing community of animals for decades, from scavenging sharks and hagfish in the first months to bacteria that slowly break down the bones.__ For this reason, biologists sometimes describe sunken whales as oases on the deep seafloor.
questions.prompt: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It explains why a whale's body sinks after the whale dies.
It presents a disagreement among biologists about how long whale carcasses last.
It describes the method biologists use to find whale carcasses on the seafloor.
It describes how a sunken whale supports life over a long period, which explains the description in the last sentence.
questions.explanation: The underlined sentence shows a carcass feeding many animals for decades, and the last sentence ("For this reason") calls sunken whales oases because of that.

questions.passage:
**Text 1**
Some city officials argue that building new metro lines is the best way to reduce traffic on crowded streets, since a single train can carry far more passengers than a bus.

**Text 2**
A study of twelve mid-sized cities found that adding lanes reserved for buses reduced traffic nearly as much as building new metro lines did. The bus lanes cost a small fraction as much and took months, rather than years, to complete.
questions.prompt: Based on the texts, how would the authors of the study in Text 2 most likely respond to the officials in Text 1?
choices: By agreeing that metro lines are the only effective way to reduce traffic
By suggesting that bus lanes may reduce traffic almost as well as metro lines while costing less and taking less time to build
By arguing that a bus can carry more passengers than a train
By claiming that traffic in mid-sized cities cannot be reduced
questions.explanation: The study found bus lanes nearly as effective as metro lines but cheaper and faster, which challenges the claim that metro lines are the best option.

questions.passage: Corals get most of their food from tiny algae that live inside their tissues and use sunlight to make sugars. When the water becomes too warm, corals push out these algae and turn white, a process called bleaching. If the warm conditions last too long, the corals can starve.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Because corals depend on algae for food, losing the algae during warm periods can threaten the corals' survival.
Coral reefs grow only in warm, shallow water.
Bleaching makes corals more colorful by adding new algae.
Algae harm corals by taking sugars from them.
questions.explanation: The text explains that algae feed corals, warm water makes corals lose them, and the corals can then starve.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a poem about a city at night.

The trams lie sleeping in their sheds,
their windows dark, their bells grown still;
only the river keeps on talking
as streetlamps climb the quiet hill.
Soon the first car's rattling wheels
will wake the bakers, then the rest,
but for this hour the city sleeps
the way a tired child sleeps best.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The speaker complains that the city's trams are too noisy at night.
The speaker describes a brief period of quiet in the city before the activity of morning begins.
The speaker explains how the city's bakers prepare bread before dawn.
The speaker mourns the closing of the city's tram system.
questions.explanation: The trams are still and only the river "talks," but "Soon" the first tram will wake everyone. The poem captures a quiet hour before morning. The trams will run again, so the system has not closed.

questions.passage: A music teacher hypothesizes that students who practice in several short sessions each day improve faster than students who practice for the same total amount of time in a single long session.
questions.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the teacher's hypothesis?
choices: Students who practiced for more total time each day improved more than students who practiced for less time.
Most students said they preferred short practice sessions to long ones.
Students who practiced in the morning played more accurately than students who practiced at night.
Over eight weeks, students who practiced in three 20-minute sessions each day improved more than students who practiced in one 60-minute session each day.
questions.explanation: This finding compares short and long sessions with the same total time (60 minutes a day), which is exactly what the hypothesis is about. The choice about total time changes a different variable.

questions.passage: Marine ecologist Fenna Albers claims that young reef fish use the sounds of a healthy reef, such as the snapping of shrimp and the grunts of fish, to find a place to settle.
questions.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Albers's claim?
choices: Healthy reefs were found to be louder than damaged reefs, especially at night.
Young fish settled more often on reefs with many hiding places than on reefs with few.
Adult fish on healthy reefs produced more grunts than adult fish on damaged reefs.
When researchers played recordings of a healthy reef through underwater speakers on patches of dead coral, more young fish settled on those patches than on similar patches where no sound was played.
questions.explanation: With sound as the only difference, more young fish settled where it played, so the fish are responding to reef sounds. Knowing that healthy reefs are louder doesn't show that young fish use the sound.

questions.passage: A student notes that attendance at a city's summer jazz festival more than doubled between 2021 and 2024: ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: attendance rose from 5,900 in 2022 to 7,300 in 2023.
attendance rose from 3,900 in 2021 to 8,150 in 2024.
attendance rose from 3,900 in 2021 to 5,900 in 2022.
questions.explanation: The claim compares 2021 with 2024, and 8,150 is more than twice 3,900 (twice 3,900 is 7,800).

questions.passage: Copper roofs are reddish brown when new, but over many years they turn green as the copper reacts with moisture and gases in the air, forming a thin coating called a patina. Because this coating protects the copper underneath from further damage, architects who choose copper roofs can expect them to ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: stay reddish brown for as long as the building stands.
last for a long time without needing to be replaced.
need frequent repainting to keep them from rusting.
become thinner each year as the patina wears away.
questions.explanation: A coating that protects the copper from damage means the roof lasts a long time. The text says the roofs turn green, so they don't stay reddish brown.

questions.passage: In the early tenth century, the physician al-Razi wrote a treatise describing smallpox and measles as two separate diseases, carefully listing the early signs of each. Earlier medical writers had often described the two illnesses together or confused one with the other. Al-Razi's treatise would therefore most likely have helped physicians ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: prevent both diseases with a single treatment.
show that measles is more dangerous than smallpox.
tell patients with one of the diseases apart from patients with the other.
diagnose patients without examining their symptoms.
questions.explanation: Listing the signs of each disease separately, where earlier writers confused them, would help doctors tell the two illnesses apart.

questions.passage: Because the museum's main hall was being ______ the exhibition of Central Asian textiles moved to a smaller gallery for the summer.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: A comma separates the introductory "Because..." clause from the main sentence.

questions.passage: The city's new tram cars are longer than the old ______ their lighter frames, however, let them use less electricity.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: Both parts are complete sentences, so they need a semicolon. "However" can't join two sentences, so a comma alone creates a comma splice.

questions.passage: The engineers faced one major obstacle in designing the new ______ soft riverbank clay that could not support heavy foundations.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: A colon after a complete sentence introduces the explanation of what the obstacle was. A semicolon would need a complete sentence after it.

questions.passage: Aerogel, a solid that is mostly ______ is one of the lightest materials ever made.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The phrase "a solid that is mostly air" interrupts the sentence and opens with a comma, so it must close with a comma too.

questions.passage: The nest that a pair of storks built on top of the old minaret ______ nearly two meters across.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The subject is the singular "nest," not "storks," so the verb is **is**.

questions.passage: The researchers hope that by ______ coral fragments on underwater frames, they can speed the recovery of the damaged reef.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: After the preposition "by," the verb takes the -ing form: **growing**.

questions.passage: Both ______ designs for the new pedestrian bridge included separate lanes for bicycles.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: "Both" means there are two architects, and the designs belong to them, so the plural possessive **architects'** is needed.

questions.passage: Sound loses energy much more slowly as it travels through water than as it travels through air. ______ the low calls of some whales can be heard by other whales hundreds of kilometers away.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: Whales hearing each other far away is a result of sound losing energy slowly in water.

questions.passage: Many early jazz musicians learned to play by ear rather than by reading written music. ______ some of the era's best-known bandleaders read music fluently and wrote out detailed arrangements for their orchestras.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: Bandleaders who read music fluently contrast with musicians who played by ear.

questions.passage: Building the new metro line required closing several busy streets for months. ______ the city ran free shuttle buses along the affected routes until construction was finished.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: The free buses were the city's reaction to the street closures, so **In response** fits.

Some subway lines in Paris and Mexico City use trains with rubber tires.
Rubber tires wear out faster and produce more heat than steel wheels.
Most subway trains run on steel wheels on steel rails.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Cork is the bark of the cork oak, a tree that grows mainly in Portugal and Spain.
• Workers strip the bark by hand without cutting down the tree.
• The bark grows back and can be harvested again about every nine years.
• Cork is light and springy because its cells are filled with air.

choices: Cork, the bark of the cork oak, comes mainly from Portugal and Spain.
Cork is light and springy because its cells are filled with air.
Cork is renewable because the bark of the cork oak grows back after it is stripped and can be harvested again about every nine years.
Workers strip the bark of the cork oak by hand.

questions.passage: Historian Javlon Sharipov's biography of the poet is deliberately ______: he reports what the surviving letters and records show but declines to guess at the poet's private motives wherever the documents are silent.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Refusing to go beyond the evidence makes the biography **restrained**. *Speculative* is the opposite, and nothing suggests the book attacks anyone (*polemical*) or covers everything (*exhaustive*).

questions.passage: Although the city council voted for the tram project, its support was ______: members approved only the first section of the line and insisted that any extension depend on that section meeting its ridership targets.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Support that comes with limits and conditions is **qualified** support. *Unconditional* is the opposite of what the colon describes.

questions.passage: Composer Anvar Hakimov's arrangements of old Uzbek folk songs are anything but ______: rather than simply writing the melodies down as he heard them, he reharmonizes them, alters their rhythms, and weaves fragments of several songs into a single piece.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: "Anything but" means "not at all." Changing harmonies and rhythms is the opposite of copying the songs exactly, so the arrangements are not **literal**. They are inventive, so "anything but inventive" would say the reverse.

questions.passage: Although al-Biruni's eleventh-century estimate of Earth's radius came remarkably close to the modern value, historian of science Nilufar Azimova cautions against treating it as ______ proof of his method's precision: small errors in his measurements may have partly canceled each other out.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Azimova warns that the accurate result may partly reflect errors that canceled out, so it is not **unequivocal** (beyond doubt) proof. No warning would be needed against calling it *tentative* proof.

questions.passage: For years, a sharp rise in reports of jellyfish along certain coastlines was taken as evidence that jellyfish populations worldwide were booming, perhaps because overfishing had removed fish that compete with them for food. Marine ecologist Signe Rasmussen is not convinced. __Many of the reports, she notes, come from regions where beach monitoring and citizen-science programs began only recently, so the rise in sightings may simply reflect a rise in the number of people looking.__ Rasmussen argues that only long-term surveys using consistent methods can show whether jellyfish are truly becoming more common.
questions.prompt: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It presents evidence that confirms the claim that jellyfish populations are booming.
It identifies overfishing as the cause of the increase in jellyfish populations.
It offers an alternative explanation for evidence that has been used to support a claim.
It describes the method Rasmussen used in her own long-term survey of jellyfish.
questions.explanation: The rise in reports was used as evidence of booming populations; the underlined sentence suggests the reports rose because more people were watching. Overfishing belongs to the earlier view, and Rasmussen only calls for long-term surveys rather than describing one of her own.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a novel. Nasiba, a structural engineer, is inspecting a bridge that her grandfather helped build.

From the riverbank, the bridge looked exactly as it did in the photograph that had hung in her grandparents' hallway: three gray arches, steady and sure. Up close, Nasiba saw what the photograph could not show. Rust had bled from the bolts in long orange streaks, and a crack as thin as a hair ran along the underside of the central arch. She photographed the crack from four angles, measured it twice, and wrote the numbers in her notebook in small, careful figures, the way her grandfather had written everything.
questions.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It describes a character's childhood memories of a bridge and then explains why the bridge was built.
It contrasts two engineers' opinions about whether a bridge is safe to use.
It describes damage to a bridge and then explains how the character plans to repair it.
It presents the bridge as it appears from a distance, then reveals damage visible only up close, and finally describes the character's careful response.
questions.explanation: The text moves from the distant view, to the damage seen up close, to Nasiba's careful recording of it. She measures and records the crack but never plans a repair, which rules out the tempting last choice.

questions.passage:
**Text 1**
Many owners of historic brick buildings repair crumbling mortar with modern cement mortar, which is much stronger than traditional lime mortar and sets more quickly. A stronger mortar, they reason, will hold the bricks together longer and reduce the need for future repairs.

**Text 2**
Materials scientist Corin Abernethy points out that in a wall, mortar and brick must work together. When the mortar is harder and less porous than the old bricks around it, moisture that would normally escape through the mortar is forced out through the bricks instead, and as that water freezes and thaws, the bricks themselves crack and crumble. Soft lime mortar, Abernethy notes, is meant to be a wall's weak point: it wears away first and can be replaced, sparing the bricks.
questions.prompt: Based on the texts, how would Abernethy (Text 2) most likely respond to the reasoning of the building owners in Text 1?
choices: By agreeing that cement mortar reduces the need for future repairs but objecting to its cost
By arguing that the strength of cement mortar can itself cause damage, since it shifts wear from the mortar to the bricks, which are harder to replace
By arguing that lime mortar is actually stronger than cement mortar over long periods
By claiming that the bricks in historic buildings are not affected by moisture
questions.explanation: Text 1 assumes stronger mortar is better. Abernethy explains that hard mortar pushes moisture through the bricks and ruins them, while soft mortar is meant to wear out first. He never says lime is stronger; its value is that it is weaker.

questions.passage: Historian Paulina Ostrowska cautions that the jazz preserved on the earliest records may give a misleading picture of what dance-hall audiences actually heard. Because each side of a record held only about three minutes of music, and because early recording equipment captured loud drums and deep bass notes poorly, bands often shortened their pieces, replaced the bass drum with wood blocks or cymbals, and used a tuba in place of a string bass in the studio. The music that survives on disc, she argues, is therefore an adaptation shaped by technology rather than a straightforward record of live performance.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Early jazz bands preferred recording studios to dance halls because studios gave them more control over their sound.
Early jazz records are of little use to historians because each side holds only about three minutes of music.
Because of technical limits, early jazz bands changed their music when recording, so early records may not accurately show how the bands sounded live.
Drummers in early jazz bands were less skilled than other band members and were often left out of recordings.
questions.explanation: Ostrowska's point is that recording limits forced bands to change their music, so records differ from live shows. She calls the records adaptations, not useless, so the choice about little use goes too far.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a poem. The speaker addresses an old map of a city.

You promised streets that ran in ordered lines,
a river drawn in one sure stroke of blue,
a market standing where your legend said.
I walked your lines. The river bent where you ran straight;
the market had become a park, the park a road.
Still, I keep you folded in my coat—
not for the way, which you have long forgotten,
but for the city you remember, which I never saw.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Frustrated by the map's errors, the speaker decides to replace it with a newer one.
Although the map no longer guides the speaker accurately, the speaker values it as a record of the city as it once was.
The speaker uses the map to find the market described in its legend.
The speaker regrets that the city's river was moved to make room for a road.
questions.explanation: The map's directions no longer work ("the way, which you have long forgotten"), yet the speaker keeps it for "the city you remember." The speaker keeps the map rather than replacing it, and the market is gone.

questions.passage: Urban researcher Tamsin Achterberg studied neighborhoods near a city's new tram line, where car traffic fell after the line opened. She hypothesizes that the decline resulted mainly from existing residents switching from cars to the tram rather than from a change in who lived in the neighborhoods.
questions.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Achterberg's hypothesis?
choices: Among households that lived in the neighborhoods both before and after the line opened, the number of car trips per household fell by about a third.
After the line opened, many households that owned cars moved out of the neighborhoods and were replaced by households without cars.
Tram ridership in the neighborhoods grew steadily during the line's first year.
Car traffic in the neighborhoods fell more on weekdays than on weekends.
questions.explanation: Following the same households rules out a change in residents: if those households made far fewer car trips, they switched. The choice about car owners moving out supports the rival explanation, and rising ridership could come from new residents.

questions.passage: Researchers counted fish on four reefs in 2015 and again in 2023. Two of the reefs lie inside a marine reserve where fishing has been banned since 2015, and two lie outside it. The researchers concluded that the fishing ban likely contributed to an increase in fish numbers.
questions.prompt: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the researchers' conclusion?

Fish numbers rose on both Kestrel Reef and Marrow Bank between 2015 and 2023.
Fish numbers on both reefs inside the reserve rose by more than 25 per 100 square meters, while numbers on the reefs outside it changed by no more than 4.
In 2023, Larkspur Reef had fewer fish per 100 square meters than Kestrel Reef did.
questions.explanation: To link the ban to the increase, compare reefs inside and outside the reserve: +29 and +26 inside, but +4 and −3 outside. The other choices are true but never compare protected with unprotected reefs.

questions.passage: Cleaner wrasse are small reef fish that eat parasites off larger "client" fish, though they would rather bite off a client's protective mucus, which clients find painful. In experiments, cleaners took such bites less often when other clients were nearby and could watch. Researchers proposed that cleaners behave this way to protect their reputation, since clients that see a cleaner bite another fish tend to avoid that cleaner. If this proposal is correct, cleaners would be expected to ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: bite clients equally often whether or not other fish are watching.
bite clients mainly when parasites are scarce on the reef.
bite clients less often at busy cleaning stations, where many clients wait nearby, than at stations that few fish visit.
questions.explanation: If cleaners behave well to protect their reputation, they should cheat less where more potential clients are watching, as at a busy station. The "equally often" choice contradicts the experiment, and parasite supply plays no part in the reputation explanation.

questions.passage: Archaeologists analyzing bronze objects from an ancient settlement in Central Asia found that tools contained about 10 percent tin, the proportion that makes bronze especially hard, while decorative ornaments contained much less tin and more lead, which helps molten bronze flow into fine, detailed molds. Because both kinds of objects were made in the same workshops during the same period, the archaeologists concluded that ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: tin was likely too scarce at the settlement to be used in decorative objects.
the ornaments were likely made later, after lead had become easier to obtain.
lead likely makes bronze harder than tin does.
the metalworkers likely adjusted the makeup of their bronze to suit the purpose of each object.
questions.explanation: Each recipe matches what the object needed: hardness for tools, easy casting for detailed ornaments. The same workshops and period rule out the idea that the ornaments came later, and the ornaments did contain some tin.

questions.passage: The tenth-century mathematician Ibn ______ described the law of refraction more than six hundred years before Willebrord Snell, the Dutch scientist whose name the law usually bears.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: "Ibn Sahl" identifies which mathematician is meant, so it is not set off with punctuation, and nothing should separate the subject from its verb, "described."

questions.passage: The glaze on the new ceramic tiles resists scratches and stains. When the tiles are left in strong ______ the glaze slowly turns yellow.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: "However" interrupts the second sentence between its introductory clause ("When...sunlight") and its main clause, so it needs a comma on each side. A semicolon would split that sentence into two fragments.

questions.passage: The most surprising finding of the deep-sea survey ______ that several of the newly discovered species live more than 8,000 meters below the surface.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The clause "that several...surface" completes the verb "was," and no punctuation belongs between a verb and what completes it.

questions.passage: Cooled in liquid nitrogen, the ceramic conducts electricity with no resistance at ______ warmed to room temperature, it conducts electricity poorly.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: Each side of the blank is a complete sentence ("the ceramic conducts..." and "warmed to room temperature, it conducts..."), so a semicolon is needed. A comma, with or without *when*, still joins two sentences with only a comma.

questions.passage: Engineers designed the bridge's new cables to resist corrosion from road salt, to stretch slightly in strong winds without weakening, and ______ sensors that report any damage to a central computer.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The items in the list describe what the cables were designed to do, and the first two begin with *to* ("to resist," "to stretch"). The third must match: **to carry**.

questions.passage: If conservators had not moved the frescoes indoors in the 1970s, much of the paint ______ away by now.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: A condition about the past that did not happen ("If...had not moved") pairs with **would have** plus the past participle.

questions.passage: Unlike the paintings in the museum's east wing, which were cleaned last year, ______
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: the west wing still has paintings covered in darkened varnish.
darkened varnish still covers the paintings in the west wing.
the paintings in the west wing are still covered in darkened varnish.
there is still darkened varnish on the paintings in the west wing.
questions.explanation: The opening phrase compares the east-wing paintings with something, so the subject right after the comma must be other paintings. The other choices compare the paintings with a wing, with varnish, or with nothing.

questions.passage: Engineers once expected ceramic engines to replace metal ones, since ceramics can withstand much higher temperatures and would allow engines to burn fuel more efficiently. ______ the brittleness of ceramics, their tendency to crack under sudden stress, has largely confined them to small engine parts.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: The expectation is followed by what actually happened, which fell short of it, so **In practice** fits. *For this reason* wrongly presents brittleness as a result of the ceramics' heat resistance.

questions.passage: In the 1950s and 1960s, many cities in Europe and North America tore out their streetcar lines, viewing them as old-fashioned obstacles to automobile traffic. ______ several of those cities have since spent large sums building new tram lines, sometimes along the very streets where the old tracks were removed.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: Paying to rebuild what they once tore out is an unexpected reversal, which **Ironically** signals. *Consequently* would mean that removing the tracks caused the rebuilding.

questions.passage: Engineers expected the soft clay beneath the river to be the hardest part of the new metro tunnel to dig through. ______ the clay was excavated with little difficulty; it was a band of large boulders, missed by earlier surveys, that slowed the tunneling machines for months.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: What actually happened differed from what the engineers expected, so **As it turned out** fits. *As expected* and *Accordingly* both suggest the clay behaved as predicted.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Pianist Ilona Varga released two well-known albums, *The Nightjar Sessions* (1957) and *Desert Bloom* (1964).
• *The Nightjar Sessions* was recorded live in a crowded club in a single night.
• *Desert Bloom* was recorded in a studio over six months, and many of its pieces were assembled from several takes.
• Critics praised both albums.
questions.prompt: The student wants to contrast how the two albums were made. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Varga released *The Nightjar Sessions* in 1957 and *Desert Bloom* seven years later, in 1964.
Critics praised both of Varga's albums, *The Nightjar Sessions* and *Desert Bloom*.
*Desert Bloom*, which Varga recorded in a studio, took six months to complete.
Varga recorded *The Nightjar Sessions* live in a club in a single night, whereas she assembled *Desert Bloom* in a studio over six months.
questions.explanation: The goal is how the albums were made, which needs both recording methods. The dates contrast when, not how, and the *Desert Bloom* choice describes only one album.

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Biologist Hana Ilyasova tested whether underwater noise from ships affects how hermit crabs choose new shells.
• Crabs exposed to recorded ship noise took longer to approach a new shell than crabs exposed to ordinary ocean sounds.
• Crabs exposed to ship noise also spent less time inspecting a new shell before deciding whether to move into it.

choices: Hermit crabs live in empty snail shells, trading up to larger ones as they grow, and Ilyasova found that crabs exposed to ship noise were slower to approach a new shell and spent less time inspecting it.
Ilyasova found that crabs exposed to ship noise took longer to approach a new shell and spent less time inspecting it.
Hermit crabs live in empty snail shells, which they trade for larger ones as they grow.
Ilyasova tested whether underwater noise from ships affects how hermit crabs choose new shells.
questions.explanation: An unfamiliar audience needs to know why shells matter to hermit crabs, and the goal also requires the findings. Only this choice gives both; the other choice with the findings leaves out that background.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Al-Farabi (c. 870–950) was a philosopher and scholar from Central Asia.
• His commentaries on Greek philosophy earned him the title "the Second Teacher," after Aristotle.
• He also wrote the *Great Book of Music*.
• The book discusses the theory of musical intervals and describes instruments such as the oud.

choices: Al-Farabi's *Great Book of Music* discusses the theory of musical intervals and describes instruments such as the oud.
Al-Farabi, called "the Second Teacher" for his commentaries on Greek philosophy, also wrote the *Great Book of Music*, a study of musical intervals and instruments.
Al-Farabi earned the title "the Second Teacher," after Aristotle, for his commentaries on Greek philosophy.
